name: Felix Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live at home with my dad, so my week starts with a twenty-minute train into the city for economics and business lectures. After class I switch the delivery app on and cycle for food orders until about ten, usually four evenings. In between I use AI for everything: summarising readings, planning my week, even practising interview answers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you choose business and economics?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My nan used to say I could sell sand in a desert. I started by flipping trainers online at sixteen, and I want to understand why some businesses win. I also want to start my own thing, but I'm not sure what yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one is called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a bit of a letdown but fine. I already use it every day and it saves me an hour or two, so even a small thing is useful. I'd tell my mates the hype is bigger than the product.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved nothing wild happens, but my own situation isn't easy. I'm paid per delivery, my bike needs repairs, and the loan will be there for years. I like risks, but I can't afford many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep delivering and studying, and use AI to run my trainer-reselling side thing more smoothly: writing listings, answering buyers, setting prices. I'd try to save maybe sixty a week. I'd also look for a real internship at a small firm for the summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I want something to happen, but I can't pretend I need it to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the delivery work pay, and what happens in a bad week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get a fixed fee per order, so A rainy Tuesday can be good and a quiet Sunday can be nothing. In a bad week I might make forty, and then I have to cover the bike chain and my phone data. My dad slips me ten here and there, which I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your side business actually earn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eighty pounds a month on a good month. I keep it in a separate account and tell myself it's my starter pot. It's small, but it taught me more than a lecture on margins.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but overhyped**, and the real edge is using it well.
I'd tell friends to **start something small** now.
think: Even a quiet AI world leaves me with **loan debt** and uneven delivery pay.
I like risk, but I can't afford **many**.
do: Keep delivering and use AI to run my **trainer-reselling** side business.
Save **sixty a week** and look for a summer internship.
feel: Fine but a bit **restless**, wanting something to happen.
S0.quote: A rainy Tuesday can be good and a quiet Sunday can be nothing.
fieldNote: Felix's **adaptive side** shows in how he already uses AI to earn.
Money is thin and uneven, but he sees it as a challenge.
Dislikes taking cash from his dad.

steps.text: Keep delivering four evenings a week
Use AI to write listings for my trainer resales
Try a new AI tool for my economics notes
Put sixty a week into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one is called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change, and the people who learn it early will win. I'd tell my mates to stop using it for homework and start using it to build things. At the same time I'd say the government should make sure nobody gets left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think good news and bad news. Business graduates do a lot of writing, checking and planning, so the entry-level desk jobs may shrink. But the card says new jobs appear, and I'm already comfortable with the tools, so I could be one of the people who gets hired because of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build a small online business around something AI makes cheaper, like a service for local shops that need listings and social media. I'd use my delivery contacts, because I know every restaurant in town. I'd also take a data or coding short course, probably online at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit scared. It feels like a race and I like races.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you make a business from this, with no money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Start with one customer. I know a pizza place on my route whose owner hates doing the menu and the website. I'd do it for free the first month and then charge twenty a week. Once there are five restaurants, that's real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worst case for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That everyone does the same and it's a race to the bottom, with prices at nothing. Or that I get so busy with hustles I fail my exams and lose the degree. I know that's the risk.

say: I'd say people who **learn it early** will win.
I'd also say the government should make sure **nobody is left behind**.
think: Entry-level desk jobs may **shrink**, but I'm already comfortable with the tools.
I see a chance to get hired **because of AI skills**.
do: Build a small **service for local restaurants** with listings and social media.
Take a **data or coding** short course online at night.
feel: **Excited** and a bit scared, like a race I want to be in.
S1.quote: I know a pizza place on my route whose owner hates doing the menu and the website.
fieldNote: Turns change into a **concrete first customer**, not a vague plan.
Shows real awareness of a race to the bottom and exam risks.
Politics sit alongside hustle: he wants rules as well as chances.

steps.text: Offer a pizza place a free menu and website month
Use AI daily to draft shop listings and posts
Take an online data short course at night

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one is called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge shock and the government needs to act right now. Two years is nothing, and people like my dad aren't ready. I'd say it's exciting too, but not if people lose their jobs and housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be rattled. A lot of what I'm studying would be done by AI before I graduate, so the degree might be just a piece of paper. But I'm adaptable, so I'd be the one thinking how to use it before anyone else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on building something, quickly. I'd pour my delivery earnings into a tiny business that sells services or products using AI, and I'd talk to every business owner I know. I'd also help my dad, who is a bus mechanic and thinks he's safe, to plan for robots arriving by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dizzy. Good and bad at once. I couldn't switch off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With 2 years, how would you decide whether to stay at university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay for the first year to see what the universities do, because the loan is already in. But I'd go part time on the lectures and full time on a business. If after a year I've got paying customers, I'd probably pause the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit him down and say, Dad, the garage will be fine for a few years, but robots come in 2031, so let's save money and look at what you could do next. He'd get stubborn, but I'd say it three times.

say: I'd say it's a **huge shock** and the government must act now.
I'd say it's exciting, but not if people **lose housing**.
think: The degree could become a **piece of paper** before I graduate.
I'd be the one thinking how to **use it first**.
do: Put **delivery earnings** into a tiny AI-powered business and talk to owners.
Sit my dad down and **plan** for robots arriving in 2031.
feel: **Dizzy**, with good and bad together, unable to switch off.
S2.quote: I'd go part time on the lectures and full time on a business. If after a year I've got paying customers, I'd probably pause the degree.
fieldNote: Short warning makes him **pivot hard** to a business, even over the degree.
Worries about his dad, a bus mechanic, more than himself.
His excitement and fear are equally strong.

steps.text: Start a small AI-powered service business for shops
Spend delivery earnings on tools and a simple website
Sit my dad down to plan for 2031
Switch to part-time lectures and watch customer numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one is called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a great window if people use it well, and a disaster if they don't. I'd tell my friends to learn things that matter, like sales, negotiating and building trust. Nobody should wait for the day it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd feel okay. I'd graduate in three years with a business I've started, and I'd have two years of AI-run life. There's a decent chance I'm ahead of most people. But I'd keep in mind that anyone can fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree because the loan is there anyway, and run my business alongside. I'd find a mentor at a small company. I'd also move out of my dad's flat in a year or two, but stay close, and invest what I earn in a basic savings account and some shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly buzzing, with some nerves. It's the kind of time you can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in the first year, while you can see it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the stuff that won't matter, like the long reading nobody checks. I'd spend more time on real customers, which AI can't fake. And I'd put at least a hundred a month away, even if it means fewer deliveries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a person you'd be most worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin, who works in a call centre. He's good but he follows scripts, and scripts are what AI does. I'd tell him to move now, before the layoffs, and I'd help him write his applications.

say: I'd say five years is a **great window** if people use it well.
I'd tell friends to learn **sales and trust**.
think: I could graduate with a **business already running**, ahead of most.
Anyone can fall, including **me**, so I would keep a **cushion** and not get cocky about it.
do: Finish the degree and run my **business alongside**.
Put **a hundred a month** into savings and some shares.
S3.quote: I'd spend more time on real customers, which AI can't fake.
fieldNote: Felix is **genuinely calm** here, because time and adaptability line up.
Worried about his cousin in a call centre, who follows scripts.
Plans to invest, which fits his appetite for risk.

steps.text: Run my reselling business alongside the degree
Buy a small amount of shares each month
Save a hundred a month, even with fewer deliveries
Help my cousin write job applications

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one is called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so there's no excuse. Anyone who wants to adapt can. I'd also say we have to look after the people who can't, like my dad and my gran.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think I'm in great shape. By 2036 I'd be twenty-eight, with a decade of experience in business and AI tools. There's no sense of panic, only that I don't want to waste the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a start-up for a couple of years, then launch my own company. I'd keep reselling as a side project and try a new tool every month. I'd also help my dad buy a flat or pay down his debts, so he's not stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit impatient. I wish it were now, so I could get started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with this, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I assume I'm special and I'm not. A lot of people will be good with AI by then, so being good at it isn't enough. I'd need real skills, like selling and leading people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your gran that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That she doesn't have to learn it all, and I'll set up her tablet and show her one thing at a time. She'd say she's too old, and I'd say, you taught me to ride a bike, you can do this.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty**, so there's no excuse.
I'd say we must look after people who **can't adapt**.
think: I'd be in **great shape** at twenty-eight, with a decade of experience.
I don't want to **waste** the time.
do: Finish the degree, work for a **start-up**, then launch my own company.
Help my dad **pay down debts** so he isn't stuck.
feel: **Calm** and a bit impatient, wishing it started now.
S4.quote: I'd say, you taught me to ride a bike, you can do this.
fieldNote: Calm is **earned** by long time and strong adaptability.
Admits that being good with AI will not be a special skill.
Warm with his gran, who he would teach step by step.

steps.text: Finish the degree and join a start-up
Keep reselling trainers as a side project
Try a new AI tool every month
Set up my gran's tablet and teach her one thing at a time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything I want, a degree, a business, a stable dad, gets squeezed into a tiny space. What would help most is a plan from government, and cheap ways for young people to start things, like free business advice and simple loans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume young people are fine because we're good with phones. Being good at an app isn't the same as having money or a safety net. Some of us are cycling in the rain for forty pounds.

headlineQuote: Being good at an app isn't the same as having money or a safety net.
portrait: Felix, 18, studies **business and economics**, lives with his dad and cycles for food delivery four evenings a week.
He uses AI every day and already runs a small **trainer-reselling** business.
He's progressive and wants rules to protect people, but also sees AI as a **chance** to build something.
Thin, uneven money keeps him uneasy, and the two-year warning pushes him to pause the degree.
With five or ten years he is calm, though he worries about his dad and his gran.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because everything he wants gets squeezed into a tiny space.
whatWouldHelp: A **government plan** and cheap ways for young people to start things, like free business advice and simple loans.
